items.title: Trump calls Takaichi from Air Force One after China summit

featured_image.name: Trump speaks to Japanese Premier Takaichi after China trip

items.description:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and President Donald Trump reaffirmed an "unwavering" bilateral alliance in a phone call on Thursday evening, according to a readout from the Japanese Prime Minister's Office, as Trump flew home from a three-day summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.[1]

Trump called Takaichi from aboard Air Force One, The Japan Times reported, providing her with a "detailed explanation" of his talks with Xi. The 15-minute conversation covered China-related economic and security affairs, the war in Iran, and cooperation in the Indo-Pacific region. Both leaders agreed to continue close communication and to coordinate ahead of next month's Group of Seven summit in France.[2][1]

items.title: All 46 Council of Europe nations adopt migration declaration

featured_image.name: Ministers adopt new interpretation of migrants' rights in European legal  system | Reuters

items.description:
All 46 Council of Europe member states adopted a political declaration on migration on Friday at a meeting in Chișinău, Moldova, setting out a new interpretation of the European Convention on Human Rights that could make it easier to deport certain migrants — including to third-country "return hubs."[1][2]

The non-binding declaration, the first of its kind on migration from the Council of Europe, was adopted by foreign ministers at the 135th session of the Committee of Ministers. It reaffirms that states have what it calls an "undeniable sovereign right to control the entry and residence of foreign nationals" and that nations facing mass arrivals may pursue new approaches to deter irregular migration.[2]

items.title: CENTCOM says 72 ships redirected in Iran blockade

featured_image.name: CENTCOM boasts month-long Iran naval blockade, redirecting 67 commercial  ships

items.description:
U.S. Central Command confirmed on Friday that American naval forces have redirected 72 commercial vessels and disabled four ships since the start of a maritime blockade targeting Iranian ports around the Strait of Hormuz, as escalating confrontations at sea continued to rattle global energy markets and shipping lanes.[1][2]

The update came on a volatile day that also saw a vessel seized near the United Arab Emirates and diverted toward Iranian waters, while an Indian-flagged cargo ship, the MSV Haji Ali, sank off the coast of Oman after a suspected drone or missile strike.[3][4]

items.title: China declines Nvidia H200 chips despite US clearance, Trump says

featured_image.name: Trump: Nvidia can sell H200 chips to China for 25% U.S. share

items.description:
Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One as he returned from a state visit to Beijing, President Donald Trump said on Thursday that China has so far declined to purchase Nvidia H200 artificial intelligence chips, even though Washington has approved their sale. Trump said the issue "did come up" during his meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping but that Beijing "chose not to" buy the chips because it "wants to try and develop their own" domestic alternatives.[1]

The remarks came a day after Reuters reported that the U.S. Commerce Department had cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies — including Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance, and JD.com — to purchase H200 chips, with distributors Lenovo and Foxconn also approved to handle sales. Under the licensing terms, each approved customer may buy up to 75,000 chips, either directly from Nvidia or through authorized intermediaries. Yet not a single delivery has taken place.[2][3]

items.title: Iran seizes floating armory near Strait of Hormuz

featured_image.name: Iran seizes vessel in Strait of Hormuz, defying US naval superiority

items.description:
Iranian forces boarded and seized a vessel operating as a floating armory in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday, diverting it toward Iranian territorial waters in a move that adds a new layer of tension to an already volatile maritime corridor.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), a British military-linked maritime monitoring agency, reported that the vessel was boarded and "taken by unauthorized personnel" while anchored about 38 nautical miles northeast of Fujairah, a key oil export terminal in the United Arab Emirates. Maritime security consultancy Vanguard Tech subsequently identified the ship as the Honduras-flagged Hui Chuan, a fishing support vessel that had been operating as a floating armory — a ship used to store weapons for private security companies that protect commercial vessels from pirate attacks.[1][2][3]

items.title: US and Iran defer uranium talks, prioritize Hormuz

featured_image.name: Iran rejects US demands, uranium enrichment continues amid negotiation  breakdown

items.description:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi confirmed on Friday that Iran and the United States have agreed to defer negotiations over Tehran's enriched uranium stockpile to a subsequent phase of talks, with both sides instead prioritizing the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the lifting of the US naval blockade on Iranian ports.

The announcement, reported by Bloomberg on May 15, underscores the persistent deadlock over one of the most contentious issues in the more than two-month-old conflict: the fate of Iran's estimated 400-plus kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% purity, believed to be buried beneath nuclear facilities struck by American bombers last year.[1][2][3]

items.title: Anthropic agrees to $30B round at $900B valuation

featured_image.name: Anthropic weighs raising funds at $900B valuation, topping ...

items.description:
Anthropic has agreed to terms for a $30 billion fundraising round that would value the AI company at approximately $900 billion, according to a report by the Financial Times on Friday, nearly tripling the startup's valuation from just three months ago.[1][2][3]

The round is being co-led by Dragoneer Investment Group, Greenoaks Capital, Sequoia Capital, and Altimeter Capital, each committing $2 billion or more. The deal is expected to close as soon as the end of this month, though final terms could still shift before a formal announcement.[2][4][1]

items.title: Kyiv holds day of mourning after missile strike kills 24

featured_image.name: Kyiv observes official day of mourning for 31 killed in Russian missile and  drone strikes | Euronews

items.description:
A Russian cruise missile tore through a nine-story residential building in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district during the early hours of Thursday, May 14, killing 24 people — including three girls aged 12, 15, and 17 — in what the Ukrainian air force described as Russia's largest aerial assault since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022.[1][2][3]

Emergency workers completed their search-and-rescue operation after more than 28 hours, clearing over 3,000 cubic metres of rubble, Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko said on Telegram. Forty-eight people were injured, about 30 were pulled from the wreckage alive, and roughly 400 required psychological support, according to the Interior Ministry.[4][1]

items.title: US allies forge closer China ties as Trump wraps Beijing summit

featured_image.name: Australia declines China's offer to 'join hands' on Trump tariffs

items.description:
As President Donald Trump concluded a two-day state visit to Beijing this week, a parallel trend has drawn scrutiny from foreign policy analysts: several of Washington's closest allies have been independently building stronger trade and diplomatic relationships with China, driven by uncertainty over U.S. trade policy and sweeping tariffs.

A Council on Foreign Relations analysis published on May 14 by Clara Fong highlighted how countries including Canada, the United Kingdom, France, South Korea, and Australia have moved to diversify their economic partnerships with Beijing. The piece arrived as Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks covering trade, Iran, Taiwan, and energy purchases.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Trump leaves Beijing without Iran breakthrough after two-day Xi summit

featured_image.name: Trump leaves Beijing with few wins, many warm words for Xi

items.description: President Donald Trump departed Beijing on Friday after more than 40 hours of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping, claiming the two leaders had found common ground on Iran's nuclear ambitions and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz — but the summit ended without a clear breakthrough on how to end the 77-day-old war.[1][2]

items.title: Bessent confirms trade, investment board talks as Trump-Xi summit opens

featured_image.name: Trump will set price floors across industries to combat ...

items.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed on Thursday that U.S. and Chinese officials are actively discussing the creation of a "Board of Trade" to oversee bilateral commerce and a separate "Board of Investment" to address Chinese investment in non-sensitive sectors of the American economy, as President Donald Trump began two days of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.[1][2][3]

Bessent said the investment board would focus on "nonstrategic, nonsensitive areas where Chinese could invest," according to remarks carried by wire services on May 14. His comments came as Trump arrived in China on Wednesday for the first presidential visit to Beijing since 2017, accompanied by a delegation of roughly 17 CEOs including Elon Musk of Tesla, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Tim Cook of Apple, and Kelly Ortberg of Boeing.[4][5][2][3]

items.title: UN demands answers after Taliban detains three journalists

featured_image.name: Taliban detains three journalists in Afghanistan, UN says - AL-MONITOR: The  Middle Eastʼs leading independent news source since 2012

items.description:
The United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan on Thursday expressed "serious concern" over the detention of at least three journalists by Taliban authorities on unspecified charges, calling for clarity on the legal basis for the arrests and urging due process protections for the detained reporters.[1][2]

The detentions mark the latest crackdown on press freedom in Afghanistan, where media workers have faced growing restrictions since the Taliban returned to power in 2021. The arrests drew swift condemnation from international press freedom organizations and raised fresh alarm about the safety of journalists operating in the country.

items.title: IPC says nearly 20 million in Sudan face acute hunger

featured_image.name: Almost 20 million people in Sudan still face acute hunger, monitors say |  Reuters

items.description: Nearly 19.5 million people in Sudan — more than 40% of the population — are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, according to a new assessment released Wednesday by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, the global hunger monitoring body. The report lands as the conflict between Sudan's military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces grinds into its fourth year with no end in sight.

items.title: Trump claims Xi's 'declining nation' remark targeted Biden

featured_image.name: U.S. President Trump Meets With China's President Xi And Attends State Banquet

items.description:
As President Donald Trump wrapped up the first day of his two-day state visit to Beijing on Thursday, he took to Truth Social to reframe Chinese President Xi Jinping's characterization of the United States as a "declining nation" — casting it not as a slight against his administration but as a critique of his predecessor, Joe Biden.

"When President Xi very elegantly referred to the United States as perhaps being a declining nation, he was referring to the tremendous damage we suffered during the four years of Sleepy Joe Biden and the Biden Administration, and on that score, he was 100% correct," Trump wrote. Trump did not specify when or where Xi made the remarks. He went on to tout what he described as an "incredible rise" under his 16 months in office, citing record stock markets, foreign investment, and military strength, while expressing hope that U.S.-China relations would be "stronger and better than ever before".[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: Six Arab nations demand Iran withdraw Hormuz claims in UN letter

featured_image.name: Gulf states urge UN action to ensure Strait of Hormuz safety

items.description: Six Arab nations have sent a joint letter to the United Nations categorically rejecting Iran's assertions of new authority over the Strait of Hormuz, escalating diplomatic pressure on Tehran over its ongoing disruption of one of the world's most vital maritime corridors.

items.title: Yemen's warring sides agree to largest prisoner swap since civil war began

featured_image.name: A prisoner swap is a symbolic step towards ending the Saudi-led war in Yemen

items.description:
Yemen's internationally recognized government and the Houthi movement agreed on Thursday to release more than 1,600 conflict-related detainees, the Office of the UN Special Envoy for Yemen announced, marking the largest prisoner exchange since the country's civil war erupted over a decade ago.[1][2]

The deal was reached after 14 weeks of intensive negotiations in Amman, Jordan, and will be carried out with the International Committee of the Red Cross, which serves as co-chair of a supervisory committee established under the 2018 Stockholm Agreement.[3][2]

items.title: Trump and Xi agree Iran must not get nuclear weapons

featured_image.name: Trump-Xi China summit: Trade, Iran, Taiwan in focus

items.description:
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed during their bilateral meeting in Beijing on Thursday that Iran "can never acquire a nuclear weapon" and that the Strait of Hormuz must remain open to global commerce, according to U.S. officials — the most concrete outcomes of a two-day summit overshadowed by the more-than-two-month-old war between the United States and Iran.[1][2]

A White House official said Xi expressed opposition to any efforts to charge tolls on vessels navigating the strait and showed interest in purchasing more U.S. oil to reduce China's dependence on the Middle East waterway, Bloomberg reported. China's official readout of the meeting, however, did not include energy among the topics the two presidents discussed, though it noted they talked about the Middle East.[3][4]

items.title: Bolivian miners clash with police in La Paz, demand president's resignation

featured_image.name: Bolivia miners clash with police, explosions rock La Paz as unrest grows |  Reuters

items.description: Explosions rocked Bolivia's administrative capital on Thursday as mining groups marched through La Paz and clashed violently with police while demanding the resignation of President Rodrigo Paz, Reuters reported. Witnesses observed protesters hurling what appeared to be sticks of dynamite as they attempted to force their way into Plaza Murillo, the central square that houses key government buildings.[1][2][3]

items.title: Lebanon demands ceasefire as third round of Israel talks open

featured_image.name: TOPSHOT-LEBANON-ISRAEL-IRAN-US-WAR

items.description:
Lebanon opened a third round of direct talks with Israel in Washington on Thursday with a demand that Israel halt military operations, as a U.S.-brokered truce set to expire on Sunday has failed to stop weeks of deadly fighting between Israel and Hezbollah.

The two-day negotiations, facilitated by U.S. officials at the State Department, bring together Lebanese envoy Simon Karam and Israeli envoy Ron Dermer, according to the schedule confirmed by the State Department last week. The talks follow previous rounds held on April 14 and April 23, when President Trump brokered the original ceasefire on April 16 and later extended it by three weeks.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Protests erupt in Havana as Cuba runs out of diesel

featured_image.name: Protests flare across Havana as power cuts deepen amid ...

items.description:
Cuba's energy minister confirmed on Wednesday that the island has completely exhausted its diesel and fuel oil supplies, a stark admission that triggered street protests across Havana as residents endured blackouts lasting more than 20 hours a day.

"We have absolutely no diesel," Vicente de la O Levy said during a special televised address, warning that the country's power grid had entered a "critical state." The minister said the Russian oil donation that arrived in late March — roughly 100,000 tonnes of crude — had been fully consumed by early May, leaving Cuba without any meaningful fuel buffer.[1][2][3]
